title: Odd and even permutations
objectives: Find a permutation’s sign, and show why the 15-puzzle cannot always be solved.

screens.title: The 15-puzzle
screens.prose: Fifteen tiles slide on a 4 by 4 board; a tile next to the blank may slide into it. This board is solved except that 14 and 15 are swapped. Try a loop of slides that brings the blank back home.
screens.question: Make four slides that return the blank to the bottom-right corner.

ops.label: Swap 14 and 15
ops.why: Tiles only slide into the blank square, so two tiles cannot swap directly.

hints.text: Move the blank round the small square above and to its left.
Slide 12 down, then 11 right.
Then 14 up and 12 left: the blank is home.

feedback.correct: The blank is home, but 11, 12 and 14 have cycled, and 14 and 15 are still swapped.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Move the blank round a square of four cells.

explain.text: A loop of four slides cycled three tiles and left 14 and 15 as they were. Every loop we try does something like this. The next screens show why.

screens.title: Can it be solved?
screens.prose: A swap of two entries is a **transposition**. Each slide swaps the blank with one tile, so it is a transposition of the 16 squares.
screens.question: Can slides turn this board into the solved board?

options.text: No. The slides can never swap 14 and 15 alone.

options.why: You trusted that enough slides reach anything. An invariant, as in `contests` l8, rules this board out.

options.text: Yes: slide 14 and 15 past each other through the blank.
options.why: You moved both through the blank. Each pass also moves the blank, which then has to come home.

hints.text: Look for something every slide changes in the same way.
Count transpositions: each slide is one.
The sign of the permutation is the invariant; this lesson proves it.

feedback.correct: Right. This lesson proves it with the **sign** of a permutation.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what every slide does.

explain.text: It cannot be solved. Each slide is one transposition, and we will show that parity, even or odd, never changes its meaning. The swap of 14 and 15 has the wrong parity.

screens.title: Cycles into transpositions
screens.prose: Every $k$-cycle is a product of $k - 1$ transpositions: $(a_1\,a_2 \dots a_k) = (a_1\,a_k) \cdots (a_1\,a_3)(a_1\,a_2)$. Check the smallest case, $(1\,2\,3) = (1\,3)(1\,2)$.
screens.question: Where does $(1\,3)(1\,2)$ send 1, 2 and 3? Apply $(1\,2)$ first.

hints.text: Right to left: (1 2) first, then (1 3).
$1 \to 2$ under $(1\,2)$, and $(1\,3)$ leaves 2.
$2 \to 1 \to 3$ and $3 \to 3 \to 1$.

byKey.r1c1: 2 goes to 1 under $(1\,2)$, then $(1\,3)$ sends 1 to 3.

explain.text: $1 \to 2$, $2 \to 3$, $3 \to 1$, so $(1\,3)(1\,2) = (1\,2\,3)$: a 3-cycle is 2 transpositions. Counting all cycles, fixed points too, $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma = (-1)^{n - c}$.

screens.title: Parity is well defined
screens.prose: An **inversion** of a one-line permutation is a pair of positions $i < j$ whose entries are out of order. We show that no permutation is both a product of an even and of an odd number of transpositions.
screens.question: Order the proof. Leave out the false line.

lines.text: Swapping two neighbouring entries changes the inversion count by exactly 1: only that pair changes order.
A transposition of positions $p < q$ is $2(q - p) - 1$ neighbour swaps: carry one entry across, then the other back.
$2(q - p) - 1$ is odd, so every transposition flips the parity of the inversion count.
A product of $m$ transpositions has inversion count of parity $m$, since the identity has 0.
So no permutation is both a product of an even and of an odd number of transpositions.
A transposition changes the inversion count by exactly 1.
lines.why: You treated every swap as a neighbour swap. Swapping the ends of $(1, 2, 3)$ gives $(3, 2, 1)$, with 3 inversions, not 1.

hints.text: Start with the simplest swap, of two neighbours.
Build any transposition from neighbour swaps and count them.
Neighbour, count, odd, parity of m, conclude.

feedback.correct: That is the proof. So $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma = +1$ (even) or $-1$ (odd) is well defined.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Begin with a neighbour swap.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: Each neighbour swap changes the inversion count by 1, and each transposition uses an odd number of them. So the parity of the number of transpositions matches the parity of the inversion count, which is fixed.

screens.title: Two ways to the sign
screens.prose: For l8's $\sigma = (1\,5\,4)(2\,3\,8)(6\,7)$, $n - c = 8 - 3 = 5$, so $\sigma$ is odd. Check it by counting inversions in the one-line form $5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 6, 2$.
screens.question: How many inversions does $\sigma$ have?

hints.text: For each entry, count the later entries smaller than it.
Entry 5 has four smaller entries after it: 3, 1, 4 and 2.
The counts are 4, 2, 5, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, which sum to 15.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count, for each entry, the smaller entries to its right.

byKey.five: You gave $n - c$. That has the same parity, but the inversion count is 15.
byKey.half: You counted every pair. Count only the pairs out of order.

explain.text: The counts $4 + 2 + 5 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 15$. Odd, as $n - c = 5$ predicted: $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma = -1$.

screens.title: The permutation matrix
screens.prose: The permutation matrix of $\sigma$ has a 1 in row $k$, column $\sigma(k)$. It is the identity matrix with its rows rearranged. In `elimination` l10 each row swap flipped the sign of the determinant.
screens.question: What is the determinant of $\sigma$'s permutation matrix?

options.text: $-1$, since $\sigma$ is a product of an odd number of transpositions
$+1$, since every permutation matrix is invertible
options.why: You confused invertible with determinant 1. Each row swap multiplies the determinant by $-1$.
You looked at the zeros. Each row and column holds one 1, so the matrix is invertible.

hints.text: Each transposition is one row swap.
$\sigma$ is a product of 5 transpositions.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count row swaps from the identity.

explain.text: Five row swaps from $\mathbf{I}$ give $\det = (-1)^5 = -1$, which is $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma$. In general the determinant of a permutation matrix is the sign.

screens.title: The invariant
screens.prose: Now prove the 15-puzzle board cannot be solved. Colour the board like a chessboard and treat the blank as a 16th tile.
screens.question: Order the argument. Leave out the false line.

lines.text: Each slide swaps the blank with a tile: a transposition of the 16 squares.
Each slide moves the blank to a square of the other colour.
With the blank back home, its colour is the same, so an even number of slides was made.
So the reachable arrangements with the blank home are even permutations.
Swapping 14 and 15 alone is one transposition, which is odd, so it is unreachable.
The blank has moved, so anything is reachable.
lines.why: You took movement for freedom. Each slide changes the sign, and the blank's colour counts the slides.

hints.text: Each slide is a transposition.
The blank changes colour at every slide.
Transposition, colour, even count, even permutation, the swap is odd.

feedback.correct: That is the proof. The sign is an invariant.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Link the slides, the colours and the parity.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the argument needs.

explain.text: Returning the blank home takes an even number of slides, so an even permutation. A single swap is odd, so no sequence of slides makes it. This is `contests` l8's invariant idea.

screens.title: How many boards?
screens.prose: Only even arrangements with the blank home can be reached, and a theorem says every one of them can. So, letting the blank roam too, exactly half of all arrangements of the 16 squares are reachable. $16! = 20{,}922{,}789{,}888{,}000$.
screens.question: How many arrangements can be reached from the solved board?

options.why: You took all $16!$ arrangements. The odd half can never be reached.
You halved twice. The sign splits the arrangements into two halves, not four.

hints.text: The sign splits the arrangements into two equal halves.

feedback.correct: Right: $16!/2$. On a 2 by 3 board a search reaches 360 of the 720 arrangements, also half.

explain.text: $16!/2 = 10{,}461{,}394{,}944{,}000$. A breadth-first search of the smaller 2 by 3 puzzle reaches 360 of its $6! = 720$ arrangements, confirming the half.

screens.title: Is a 3-cycle odd?
screens.prose: A 3-cycle moves three entries, and a transposition moves two.
screens.question: Is the 3-cycle $(1\,2\,3)$ even or odd?

options.text: Odd: it moves 3 things, and 3 is odd.
options.why: You counted the entries moved. The sign counts transpositions: a $k$-cycle is $k - 1$ of them.

options.text: Neither: only transpositions have a sign.
options.why: You limited the sign to transpositions. Every permutation is a product of them, so every one has a sign.

hints.text: Write it as transpositions.
Two transpositions: even. A 4-cycle needs three: odd.

feedback.correct: Right. A $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$: a 3-cycle is even and a 4-cycle is odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count transpositions, not entries.

byKey.odd: You read the length as the parity. A $k$-cycle is $k - 1$ transpositions, so $(1\,2\,3)$ is even.

explain.text: $(1\,2\,3) = (1\,3)(1\,2)$, two transpositions, so it is even. A 4-cycle is three transpositions, so it is odd. The identity is even, with zero.

screens.title: The alternating group
screens.prose: The sign turns products into products: $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau) = \operatorname{sgn}\sigma \operatorname{sgn}\tau$, since transposition counts add. l10 calls such a map a homomorphism. So the even permutations form a subgroup $A_n$. Exactly half of $S_n$ is even, for $n \ge 2$.
screens.question: How many elements does $A_4$ have?

hints.text: Half of them are even.

byKey.all: You counted all of S4. Only the even half is in A4.
byKey.quarter: You divided by 4. The sign splits S4 into two halves.

explain.text: Multiplying by $(1\,2)$ pairs each even permutation with an odd one, so $|A_n| = n!/2$. So $|A_4| = 12$ and $|A_5| = 60$. In $S_1$ there is nothing odd.

screens.title: Rank correlation
screens.prose: A signal ranks five stocks 1 to 5. Their realised returns rank them $(2, 1, 4, 5, 3)$. A pair the two rankings order differently is **discordant**: it is an inversion. Kendall's $\tau = 1 - \tfrac{4D}{n(n - 1)}$ for $D$ discordant pairs.
screens.question: Fill in the discordant pairs $D$ and Kendall's $\tau$.

hints.text: List the inversions of 2, 1, 4, 5, 3.
The pairs (2, 1), (4, 3) and (5, 3) are out of order.

feedback.correct: Right: $D = 3$ and $\tau = 0.4$. Three inversions: the ranking is an odd permutation.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the inversions of the return ranks.

byKey.pairs: You counted all 10 pairs. Only the pairs out of order count.

explain.text: The inversions are $(2, 1)$, $(4, 3)$ and $(5, 3)$, so $D = 3$ and $\tau = 1 - 12/20 = 0.4$. The parity of $D$ is the sign, here odd.

screens.title: The sign by cycles
screens.prose: Write `sign(perm)` for a 0-based one-line tuple, from $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma = (-1)^{n - c}$ with $c$ counting every cycle, fixed points too. Do not sort. The starter forgets the fixed points. Passing these cases settles these permutations only.
screens.question: Fix sign so that it counts every cycle.

tests.name: out52
tests.setup: out = tuple(2 * k % 51 if k < 51 else 51 for k in range(52))

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 9 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly.

hints.text: Count a cycle for every unvisited start, fixed points included.
$n - c$ is the number of transpositions needed, up to parity.
Return (-1) ** (len(perm) - c).

feedback.correct: All nine pass. The 52-card out-shuffle is odd.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Read the first failing row.

explain.text: The starter's $(-1)^{c'}$, with $c'$ the moved cycles, is right exactly when an even number of them have odd length. It fails the 3-cycle $(1, 2, 0)$ and the 5-cycle, which are even.

ideas: A $k$-cycle is $k - 1$ transpositions, so $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma = (-1)^{n - c}$, fixed points counted in $c$.
Every transposition changes the inversion count by an odd number, so the sign is well defined.
The even permutations form $A_n$ with $n!/2$ elements; the 15-puzzle with 14 and 15 swapped is odd, so unreachable.
summary.trap: A 3-cycle is even: $(1\,2\,3) = (1\,3)(1\,2)$. A 4-cycle is odd.

quiz.question: A **derangement** fixes no item: hats handed back at random with nobody getting their own (`puzzles` l5-hats). Fill in the counts for 4 items.

feedback.correct: Right: 6 odd 4-cycles and 3 even double swaps, 9 in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List the cycle types with no fixed point.

byKey.fact: You counted all 24 orderings of 1 to 4. Each 4-cycle can be written 4 ways, so there are 6.

explain.text: With no fixed point, 4 items form one 4-cycle or two swaps. There are 6 odd 4-cycles and 3 even double swaps, so $6 + 3 = 9$ derangements.

quiz.question: What is the sign of the identity?

options.text: $+1$: it is a product of zero transpositions.

options.why: You counted (1 2)(1 2) as odd. That is 2 transpositions: even.

options.text: It has no sign, since it moves nothing.
options.why: Zero transpositions is an even number.

explain.text: The identity is the empty product, 0 transpositions, so it is even. Writing it as $(1\,2)(1\,2)$ uses 2, also even.

byKey.all: You counted all of S5. Halve it.
